summary: Jesus calls His disciples to store treasure in heaven, to trust their Father instead of worrying, to stop judging others, and to ask God boldly.
key_insight: The teaching on worry begins with “Therefore” (6:25). It follows straight from “You cannot serve God and mammon.” Worry about food and clothing belongs with the divided heart of verse 24, and Jesus answers it with a Father who knows what His children need.
story: “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal.” Treasure stored in heaven is safe from all of them. “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” {Mt}
The eye is the lamp of the body: a good eye fills the whole body with light, a bad eye with darkness. And no one can serve two masters. “You cannot serve God and mammon.” {Mt}

“Therefore I say to you, do not worry about your life.” Look at the birds of the air: they do not sow or reap, yet the heavenly Father feeds them. Consider the lilies of the field: even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these. If God clothes the grass that is burned tomorrow, will He not much more clothe them? “But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you.” Tomorrow can worry about itself. {Mt}

“Judge not, that you be not judged.” {Mt} Condemn not, forgive, give, and it will be given back in good measure, “pressed down, shaken together, and running over.” {Lk} Jesus asked, “Can the blind lead the blind? Will they not both fall into the ditch?” {Lk} Why look at the speck in your brother’s eye and ignore the plank in your own? First remove the plank, “and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.”
Yet disciples must not be naive: “Do not give what is holy to the dogs; nor cast your pearls before swine.” {Mt}

“Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.” If an earthly father will not give his son a stone when he asks for bread, “how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!” Then Jesus gathered it all up: “whatever you want men to do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.” {Mt}
differences: Matthew’s section is much longer. Luke parallels only the teaching on judging here (Luke 6:37–42) and records the sayings on treasure and worry in another setting (Luke 12:22–34).
Luke adds “Condemn not,” “Forgive,” and “Give,” with the picture of a measure “pressed down, shaken together, and running over.”
Luke alone includes the blind leading the blind and “A disciple is not above his teacher” at this point.
Only Matthew has the warning about dogs and swine and, in this sermon, ask, seek and knock (Luke records it in 11:9–13).

scene.label: Moth and rust
scene.text: Wealth was often kept as fine clothing, which moths could ruin, or as grain and coins. The word translated “rust” means eating, anything that eats away. Thieves could break in by digging through a wall of mud brick.

scene.label: Mammon
scene.text: An Aramaic word for wealth or possessions. Jesus speaks of it as a rival master that demands service, not as a neutral tool.

scene.label: Lilies and the oven
scene.text: The lilies were probably the bright wildflowers that cover the hills of Galilee in spring. Once dry, grass and flowers were burned as fuel in clay ovens. God clothes even something that short-lived in beauty.

scene.label: Speck and plank
scene.text: The carpenter’s son from Nazareth (Matthew 13:55) used a builder’s exaggeration: a beam of wood in one eye, a splinter in the other. The picture is meant to be absurd, and the absurdity makes the point.

scene.label: The Golden Rule
scene.text: Jewish teaching before Jesus gave a negative form: do not do to others what you hate (Tobit 4:15). Jesus states it positively, which asks far more: not only avoiding harm but doing the good you would want done to you.

witnesses.matthew: Gathers the teaching on treasure, worry, judging and prayer into one stretch of the sermon. For Matthew, the King’s people live free of greed and anxiety because they seek first “the kingdom of God and His righteousness,” and he closes the body of the sermon with the Golden Rule as the sum of “the Law and the Prophets.”
witnesses.luke: Keeps the teaching on judging and surrounds it with mercy: condemn not, forgive, give. Luke’s overflowing measure and his warning about blind guides speak to disciples who will one day lead others (6:39–40).

seeing.reveals: Jesus knows the Father so well that He can point to birds and wildflowers as evidence of His care. He also sees the human heart clearly: where the treasure goes, the heart follows.
seeing.living: Look at what you spend, save and worry about most, and ask which master it shows you serving. Then pray as a child asks a father, expecting good things, and measure others with the mercy you hope God will measure to you.
seeing.ponder: What worry are you carrying today that shows you are not sure the Father knows what you need?

preaching.big_idea: Serve God, not money, and trust your Father with what you need.
outline: Why worry with such a Father? (25–34)
preaching.watch_for: “Worry” or “worrying” comes six times in verses 25–34, three times in the command “do not worry” (vv. 25, 31, 34). The one positive command in the middle, “seek first” (v. 33), is the cure.
